World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Lessons should have been learned prior to NDIS rollout, integrity boss says
World.content:
About $3.7 billion of National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) money was handed out inappropriately last financial year, and governments have not learned from earlier mistakes when designing new programs, the scheme's integrity chief says.

John Dardo, head of integrity transformation at the NDIS, told a parliamentary inquiry into the scheme about 8.3 per cent of the $45 billion in payments made last financial year could be attributed to "integrity leakage".

That phrase was described as being broader than just fraud and included other forms of misuse such as "inadvertent non-compliance".

Mr Dardo said the scheme did not measure the amount attributable to the "technical definition" of fraud alone.

The hearing comes a week after the federal government unveiled a dramatic overhaul of the scheme, including the removal of about 160,00 participants, that it says will save $22 billion over the next four years.

The NDIS is projected to cost more than $50 billion this financial year, and reports of fraud and criminal rorts, particularly from providers, have seen the scheme take a major reputational hit.

Last week, federal minister Mark Butler said many of the problems with the scheme were a result of its design.

Today, Mr Dardo said many of those problems were repeating mistakes governments had made in other programs and were lessons governments should have learned by now.

He said the rolling out of the scheme was "rushed", too many payment claims were unverified, enforcement was "lacking", integrity was not resourced enough and those responses focused on reaction instead of prevention.

"A lot of these things we have seen in government programs before," Mr Dardo said.

" But we see those mistakes repeated as new government programs are set up and we probably need a better way of ensuring those learnings are built into government programs as they're set up from day one. "

How did the NDIS get so expensive? With more changes surrounding the NDIS just announced, here's everything you need to know about the scheme.

Mr Dardo told the hearing the NDIS' Fraud Fusion Taskforce, set up in 2022, had led to 25 successful prosecutions, with 15 others currently before the courts and more than 600 active investigations ongoing.

He said more than 2,500 providers had been removed from the NDIS because of the task force, which draws on resources from 24 other agencies, including state and territory police.

Mr Dardo said a wider fraud crackdown was producing results, with 77 warrants issued last year, compared to a combined 30 across 2018 to 2021.

The parliamentary inquiry was set up in March after NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister requested the cross-party committee probe the extend of fraud and non-compliance in the scheme.

NDIS figures at a glance The NDIS now supports more than 760,000 participants, close to double the original estimate

Spending has been projected to reach $53.4 billion this year, close to the $59 billion for defence

The government projects the latest suite of changes could save $22 billion over the next four years

The scheme is growing at 10.3 per cent per year, down from more than 22 per cent under the Coalition, but still making it the second fastest growing form of federal expenditure

The government wants annual growth at around 5-6 per cent

Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission executive Adam Meyer said "higher end" organised crime groups either based offshore or with a presence offshore were increasingly exploiting not just the NDIS, but government programs more broadly.

"They are involved in a range of activities. NDIS is one. In some cases, it's directly linked to the funding that they are obtaining through that they are recycling into other criminal activities," Mr Meyer said.

"But in many cases, they're not just targeting the NDIS. It's part of their broader business model."

Bureaucrats revealed the most significant forms of non-compliance in the scheme were services not being provided, claiming for weekend rates instead of weekdays, and the "rapid drawdown of funds that would be inconsistent with somebody being able to purchase or receive that service so quickly".

They also said the majority of participants and providers were doing the right thing.

Staff from the agency that runs the NDIS have also been involved in fraud, including undisclosed conflicts of interest and unlawful disclosure of protected information, according to a submission from the Department of Health, Disability and Aging.

The department is set to speak at the inquiry later today.

While fraud remains a significant target for the government, it is not a major driver of the scheme's overall growth.

The inquiry will report on July 2.

World.title: How a future Bronco hero Jesse Southwell broke Queensland's heart
World.content:
Just days before beginning her quest to become one of Brisbane's new heroes, Jesse Southwell was Queensland's cruellest heartbreaker.

The New South Wales halfback made the difference in yesterday's State of Origin series opener with a 65th-minute field goal that broke the deadlock en route to an 11-6 victory in Newcastle.

It was the first drop goal the 21-year-old has landed in a game in her entire life and, with Southwell moving from Newcastle to Brisbane this very weekend, a fitting farewell to the only rugby league home she has ever known.

The two plays that flipped the script on Women's State of Origin Game I With Queensland on the verge of another classic ambush, it took two "Origin plays" for New South Wales to turn the tide in the women's series opener in Newcastle.

"I've never kicked a field goal in a real game before. It was (Olivia) Kernick; we had a discussion earlier about setting up for a field goal," Southwell said.

"She told me to go for the first one. I missed it, and the second one, she said, 'Jesse, kick it now!' I was like, 'sweet' and I had lots of time.

"I don't think I've ever kicked one in any game. It was a good time to start.

"But you practice them all the time, so you know what's coming. You can put that kind of pressure on yourself at training; six-all, in a State of Origin game, minute to go, you have to get it to win. You put that in your brain when you kick it at training.

"I move on Sunday. We have some stuff next week for Bronx. I've been flying up and back."

The field goal will be Southwell's last rugby league act in the Hunter until who knows when — Brisbane are not scheduled to play Newcastle away in this year's NRLW regular season.

But despite Southwell leading the Knights to two premierships, capturing Origin glory at home was a longtime coming, given Queensland had won the previous two matches in the Hunter.

"It was really cool, really surreal, to be at home and have a good game with the girls and break that streak. We've (NSW) lost here a few times, so it's good," Southwell said.

Jesse Southwell is the NRLW's future, and the heart of Newcastle's all-conquering present Having led the Newcastle Knights to an NRLW premiership at just 17 years old, Newcastle's Jesse Southwell has the potential to be the NRLW's face for a decade, writes Nick Campton.

"It was still five minutes left, and I knew the game wasn't over yet. Queensland have done it to New South Wales in the men's and the women's time and time again.

"I was just thinking about my next job, and not losing the game from there."

The pressure on Southwell in Brisbane, which is coming off a premiership win of its own, will be immense, but that is nothing new for her.

Since she burst onto the scene in 2022 as a 17-year-old, expectations have always been heightened when it comes to her career.

She is among the first of a generation of players who are pure footballers, and she has it in her to be the best of them.

A game like yesterday's, where chances were hard to come by, but Southwell came up with the key play when it counted most, is as important a part of the journey as the masterclasses.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It is also proof that for Southwell, be it for New South Wales or Brisbane, and despite her many achievements thus far, the best is yet to come.

"I think we have a lot to improve on. Personally, as the half, there's a lot I can clean up," Southwell said.

"But that's our first game of the year, our first hit out. Everyone wanted a three-game series, and we've got it, so there's a lot of cool improvement to come.

"We knew at half-time that we were actually on top. The scoreboard didn't show that, but we knew we were on top.

"The coaching staff had a lot of faith in us, the group had a lot of faith in each other. We know what we can do; we just had to stay in the grind."

World.title: Footage of Daniels's NBA fight sparks criticism of Aussie star
World.content:
Atlanta's Australian star Dyson Daniels has been ejected from Game 6 of the Hawks-Knicks NBA play-off series after sparking a melee.

Mitchell Robinson boxed out Daniels, who responded with a right elbow to the chest of his Knicks opponent.

The incident followed a pair of free throws from Anunoby that gave the Knicks a 50-point lead in the second quarter.

A scuffle ensued, sending an official to the floor as players from both teams got involved.

The Hawks' Onyeka Okongwu and Knicks' Jalen Brunson held Robinson back as the fight inched toward fans sitting courtside.

Nickeil Alexander-Walker and several coaches pulled Daniels away, including Hawks head coach Quin Snyder.

Players from both teams became involved in the altercation. (AP: Brynn Anderson)

Robinson was also ejected from the game.

The Knicks won comfortably 140-89 to claim a 4-2 series victory and eliminate the Hawks from the play-offs.

Daniels did not receive much support on X after footage of the incident was posted.

One X user referred to Daniels as the "Great Barrier Loser", which is a play on his nickname "Great Barrier Thief".

Another user referred to Daniels's behaviour as "pathetic".

The Hawks' 83-36 deficit was the largest at half-time in NBA play-off history.

It was second overall, when including regular-season games, trailing only Dallas' 77-27 lead over the Los Angeles Clippers in 2020. The Mavericks went on to win 124-73.

The Knicks will face the winner of the Boston Celtics and Philadelphia 76ers series in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

ABC/AP

World.title: Breaking: Police confirm identity of remains found in SA bushland
World.content:
South Australia Police have confirmed the remains found in bushland south of Adelaide last week have been identified as Jeffrey Robert Mundy.

The decomposed body was discovered by a bushwalker who was looking at wildlife off Mount Alma Road at Inman Valley on the Fleurieu Peninsula at about 5:30pm last Friday.

Mr Mundy was last seen by his family on Saturday, December 19, 2020 in the Seaford area, south of Adelaide.

"The disappearance of Jeff at that time was declared a major crime and was investigated by Major Crime Investigation branch under Taskforce Southern," Major Crime Investigation Branch officer-in-charge Detective Superintendent Darren Fielke said.

"Now that we have located Jeff, we will be reviewing all aspects of the initial investigation."

Mr Fielke said police believe there are people who know what happened to Mr Mundy and have offered a $200,000 reward for anyone who has information that leads to an arrest.

"It's been over five years since Jeff Mundy went missing," Detective Superindendent Fielke said.

"It's possible those people, for whatever reason, did not come forward at the time of the initial investigation.

"Over the last five years, people who did not come forward, their circumstances and their allegiances may have changed."

Rob and Belinda Mundy have pleaded with anyone with information to come forward to police. (ABC News: Sarah Maunder)

In a statement read out on behalf of Mr Mundy's family, his father Rob thanked detectives for their work.

"And to the person who found Jeff, we could never express enough gratitude to you for assisting to bring our son home," he said.

"For five-and-a-half years, our family has lived with unbearable ache, the pain of not knowing what happened to Jeff or where he was.

“The suffering and heartbreak caused by the loss of Jeffrey has impacted every body and every member of our family, and it is something that we are forced to live with each and every day."

Rob pleaded with anyone with information to come forward.

"We are grateful Jeffrey has now been found and brought home so we can lay Jeff to rest with love and the dignity he deserves," he said.

World.title: Terrorism threat level rises in UK after stabbing of two Jewish men
World.content:
Britain has raised its national terrorism threat level to "severe" from "substantial", a day after an antisemitic stabbing attack in north London, as British Prime Minister Keir Starmer says Jewish people are living in fear and vows stronger action to protect them.

The increase to the second-highest threat level out of five means a terrorist attack within the next six months is highly likely, following the stabbing of two Jewish men in the Golders Green area, the government said.

The decision was made independently by the Joint Terrorism Analysis Centre.

Loading...

Britain last faced such a threat level in November 2021, after the Liverpool Women's Hospital bombing and the killing of lawmaker David Amess, before it was lowered to "substantial" in early 2022.

The raising of the terrorism threat level could indicate a terrorist attack within the next six months is highly likely. (Reuters: Dan Kitwood)

Interior Minister Shabana Mahmood said the assessment reflected the latest intelligence and a longer-term rise in extremist threats, and was not made solely in response to the Golders Green attack.

Officials said the classification came against a spate of recent attacks in London and mounting security concerns linked to foreign states, which they said had helped fuel violence, including against the Jewish community.

Bondi royal commission's restrained report still sends a damning message The language is restrained but in its careful way the interim report of the royal commission investigating last December’s terrorist attack is still damning.

The head of counter-terrorism policing, Laurence Taylor, said Britain had been experiencing a growing terrorist threat for some time with risks coming from multiple directions.

"We are seeing an elevated threat to Jewish and Israeli individuals and institutions in the UK," Mr Taylor said in a statement, adding that police were also working "against an unpredictable global situation that has consequences closer to home, including physical threats by state-linked actors".

Police say the two victims of the stabbing, aged 76 and 34, were both in a stable condition in hospital. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

'People are scared'

Sir Keir, who has faced severe criticism from some in the Jewish community for the government's response, promised more police in Jewish areas, a crackdown on those spreading antisemitism, and new legislation to deal with state-sponsored threats from the likes of Iran.

"People are scared, scared to show who they are in their community, scared to go to synagogue and practise their religion, scared to go to university as a Jew, to send their children to school as a Jew, to tell their colleagues that they are Jewish," he said.

He had earlier been jeered and heckled by a small crowd waving banners reading "Keir Starmer Jew Harmer" when he visited Golders Green, where the latest attack took place.

Members of the Jewish community have criticised Prime Minister Keir Starmer for what they feel has been a weak response to the incident. (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

Police said the suspect in the attack, a 45-year-old British national who was born in Somalia, had a history of serious violence and mental health issues.

They confirmed he had previously been referred to the counter-radicalisation scheme Prevent in 2020, while local media reported he had served time in prison for an incident in 2008 when he stabbed an officer and a police dog.

Stronger powers needed, Sir Keir says

Amid widespread calls for more protection for Britain's small community of about 290,000 Jewish people, Sir Keir said the government would do "everything in our power to stamp this hatred out."

This included stronger powers to shut down charities promoting extremism and a clampdown on "hate preachers," he said.

Sir Keir Starmer says he will shut down charities promoting extremism and clamp down on "hate preachers". (Reuters: Hannah McKay)

The government also said it would fast-track legislation allowing the prosecution of people acting as proxies of a state-sponsored group, so they can be dealt with in the same way as spies for foreign intelligence services.

"We need stronger powers to tackle the malign threat posed by states like Iran because we know for a fact that they want to harm British Jews," the prime minister said.

A pro-Iranian government group has claimed responsibility for some recent attacks, while last month, two men were charged under Britain's existing National Security Act with being tasked by Iran to carry out hostile surveillance.

Tehran has rejected such accusations.

Protests cause anger among Jewish community

Pro-Palestinian marches, which have become commonplace since the October 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel that triggered the Gaza war, have also fuelled anger within the Jewish community.

Critics say the demonstrations have generated hostility and become a focus for antisemitism.

"If you stand alongside people who say 'Globalise the Intifada' you are calling for terrorism against Jews, and people who use that phrase should be prosecuted," Sir Keir said.

"It is racism, extreme racism, and it has left a minority community in this country, scared, intimidated, wondering if they belong."

Sir Keir Starmer says people in the UK are scared to be open about their Jewish faith. (Reuters: Stefan Rousseau)

The recent incidents in London are part of a rising number of antisemitic attacks.

I find myself weeping again for Lebanon Lebanese families have been told to flee homes that they might never be able to return to, and families are setting up tents for an uncertain and dangerous life on the streets of Beirut all because of a conflict not of their making.

Last October, two people were killed after an attack at a synagogue in the northern English city of Manchester.

A week later, two men went on trial over a plot to kill hundreds in an Islamic State-inspired gun rampage against the Jewish community.

They were found guilty in December, just over a week after the mass shooting at the Chanukah by the Sea event at Bondi Beach.

Britain's independent reviewer of terrorism legislation, Jonathan Hall, told the BBC the British attacks had become "the biggest national security emergency" since 2017 when there was a string of high-profile attacks.

Reuters

World.title: Truck driver found guilty of negligent driving over fatal crash in Canberra
World.content:
A truck driver who hit and killed a motorcyclist in Canberra's north while driving his two daughters to sport has been found guilty of negligent driving causing death.

It took a jury less than a day to find Sean Joshua Walton, 43, not guilty of culpable driving causing death, but guilty of the alternative charge following a trial which began in the ACT Supreme Court on Tuesday.

Walton was driving his Isuzu tipper truck and turned right at the intersection of Southern Cross Drive and Beaurepaire Crescent in Holt, when he crashed into a black Harley Davidson motorbike being driven by 47-year-old Craig O'Neil on June 18, 2024.

Mr O'Neil died from his injuries soon after the crash.

Walton was focused on another vehicle, court hears

In closing submissions to the jury on Thursday, prosecutor Morgan Howe said Walton had a clear and unobstructed view of oncoming traffic for a significant period before turning, but failed to keep a proper lookout.

He said Mr O'Neil was travelling within the speed limit, with his headlights on, and would have been visible as he approached the intersection.

The fatal crash occurred at the intersection of Southern Cross Drive and Beaurepaire Crescent in Holt. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

He argued Walton had been elevated in his truck, off the ground, which meant he had improved visibility compared to other road users.

The Crown argued Walton's attention was focused on a red car slowing to turn left, and that he entered the intersection without properly checking for other vehicles, including the motorcycle.

Mr Howe told the court the key issue was whether Walton's driving amounted to a "gross" departure from the standard of care expected of a reasonable driver, arguing his failure to see the motorcyclist was "significant and inexplicable".

'Tragedy of the deepest kind'

But defence barrister Kieran Ginges told the jury the crash was a "tragedy of the deepest kind" and a "tragic accident", but not criminal conduct.

He argued Walton had been carefully assessing the intersection, observing a red car with P-plates slowing to turn, and believed it was safe to proceed.

Mr Ginges said the conditions at the time — approaching dusk, with low light and dark-coloured vehicles — made the motorcycle difficult to see.

He argued the bike may have been partially obscured behind a red car ahead of it, and only became visible as that vehicle turned.

He told the jury his client was not speeding, distracted, in a rush or affected by drugs or alcohol, and had been driving a familiar route while taking his daughters to sport.

In closing submissions, the defence pointed to two eyewitness accounts describing the crash as a "freak accident" and "an honest mistake that anyone could make". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"The human eye is not a camera," Mr Ginges said, arguing drivers must constantly process multiple moving elements and can make errors of perception.

" He never saw Mr O'Neill on his bike. "

The defence also pointed to two eyewitness accounts describing the crash as a "freak accident" and "an honest mistake that anyone could make".

The jury was also shown CCTV footage from a bus travelling in the area, which the prosecution said captured the motorcycle approaching the intersection in the moments before the crash.

The prosecution also relied on a police reconstruction drive conducted in the week before the trial, arguing it supported their case that the rider would have been visible for several seconds.

But Mr Ginges argued the reconstruction did not accurately replicate the lighting conditions, weight of the vehicle and speed Walton was travelling at the time of the crash.

A date will now be set for sentencing, before Acting Justice Peter Berman.

World.title: Australian screen industry as 'intergenerational' as housing
World.content:
Preserving Australia's film and TV industry is as important as fixing the housing crisis or saving the environment.

That was one of the key messages from the 2026 Screen Forever conference, which saw key decision-makers gather on the Gold Coast to discuss the future of the industry.

"At a time when social cohesion is under significant pressure, our stories … are even more important than ever, particularly for younger generations," Screen Producers Australia CEO Matthew Deaner said, while opening the conference.

" This is as much about intergenerational equity as housing or the environment. Australian voices and Australian stories [are] worth celebrating, worth protecting, worth preserving and we are its custodians. "

The conference, now in its 40th year, opened on a high with a celebration of the Communications Legislation Amendment Bill, which passed through parliament at the end of 2025.

Industry welcomes content quotas for streamers Arts Minister Tony Burke has proposed a requirement for 10 per cent of streaming services' local expenditure to be spent on Australian film and TV. Here's what the industry thinks.

The new law forces all streamers operating in Australia with over 1 million subscribers — in 2026 this includes AppleTV, Disney+, HBO Max, Netflix, Paramount+, Prime Video and Stan — to commit to reinvesting at least 10 per cent of their total program expenditure for Australia in local productions.

"Now, it's fair to say that local content rules on streaming platforms took far too long and created unhelpful friction within our industry," Deaner said, impressing that while the laws have been passed, it would still be some time before the effect is felt by the industry and audiences.

"But I do think there's an opportunity, and an opportunity to sort of set things forward in a different way within our industry, given the battles before us."

At the box office

Australians cinemas are finally feeling a bounce back after COVID caused the industry to close overnight; the 2025 box office took in almost $1 billion dollars in a near-return to pre-pandemic levels.

It's a trend which is continuing in 2026.

Hoyts CEO Damian Keogh said the Australian box office was already up 14 per cent from this time last year.

"That's an extra 1.5 million people going on cinema visits from January to now," he said.

"The level of optimism in the cinema industry is certainly way higher than I've seen since the COVID days."

Hoyts CEO Damian Keogh (right) and Madman's Paul Wiegard at Screen Forever 40. (Supplied: Screen Producers Australia)

Keogh also said Hoyts had pre-sold more tickets to the recently released The Devil Wears Prada 2 than they did during the Barbie phenomenon in 2023 — further cementing the theory that audiences are no longer going to the movies but going to see a movie.

But while big Hollywood blockbusters and IP-forward content are creating event-watching, it remains a struggle for independent and Australian productions to crack through.

Madman CEO Paul Wiegard said local film made up just 2 per cent of the Australian box office.

"It's a very different landscape to where we were 10 years ago, in terms of just the volume of content. [The amount] of titles rolling through the doors is enormous," Wiegard said.

"Audiences turn out for singular, bold films from directors. We need to do more backing to let the artists do their thing.

"If you looked at the films at the Academy Awards this year, they were bold, singular works across the board. We need artistically led projects in addition to the broad-based family projects."

Flicking channels

While the effects of the streaming quota bill will likely not be seen for a couple of years, the legislation also included a $50 million funding boost for the ABC to put towards drama and children's programs over the next three years.

"The ABC at the moment, in terms of audiences, we're seeing real growth. The best thing for me is that Australian content is what audiences want," ABC's head of Screen Jennifer Collins said.

Collins and Foxtel and Binge director of entertainment Daniel Monaghan emphasised the need to be "noisy" in an increasingly loud landscape.

Jen Collins (middle) with Daniel Monaghan and moderator Virginia Trioli at Screen Forever 40. (Supplied: Screen Producers Australia)

"We don't want noise for noise sakes. It's not about shocking people. It's about telling a story authentically," Monaghan said.

He confirmed Binge was trying to widen its male audience.

"If you are chasing men, for instance, be unapologetic about the stories that you're telling. Don't worry if that's not for someone who's already on the platform," he said,

Collins and Monaghan expressed a desire to see more Australian comedy on their platforms.

At the other end of the streaming spectrum, Haven't You Done Well general manager Georgia Mappin is celebrating the successful launch of streaming service Grouse House.tv in April.

"I have 1,000 subscribers and they're paying for the content that they can get for free. I think that's what's cool about my 1,000 subscribers," Mappin told ABC News.

Built off the work of Australian comedy group Aunty Donna, Haven't You Done Well has branched out into shows and web series from a variety of comedians.

The production house's bypassing of the gatekeepers of traditional screen has allowed them to cultivate a growing, dedicated audience.

Haven't You Done Well Production's Georgia Mappin (left) in conversation with Screen Queensland's Julie Eckersley. (Supplied: Screen Producers Australia)

"Everyone is still talking about how we drive audience over to broadcast and I'm like, no, it's not about driving. It's about accessing audiences where they're consuming and that doesn't work in the traditional model," Mappin said.

With former partnerships with the ABC and Netflix, Mappin says Haven't You Done Well wasn't opposed to collaboration with traditional media but it wouldn't define the operation.

"We make content everywhere [our audience are] consuming the content," Mappin said.

"That's why our production company is platform agnostic, but we're genre specialists."

The future of screen in Australia

When asked what the future of content at the ABC is, managing director Hugh Marks had a firm response: Intellectual property, or IP.

"It's all about intellectual property. It's about us, and the industry, taking the right steps to create the IP that's going to create the value that's going to be able to be reinvested into our market," Marks said.

Marks also touched on his frustration at the speed at which content is produced in the industry at the moment.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks spoke on a Screen Forever 40 panel about the future of the Australian industry. (Supplied: Screen Producers Australia)

"It can be three, four, five years between what's a great idea to realisation of that onto Australian screen," he said.

"We need to bring these ideas, the ones that we really love, through faster."

Sitting on the same panel, Screen Australia's Director of First Nations Strategy and filmmaker Rachel Perkins started her peek into the future by looking at the progress which has been made.

First Nations film Wolfram writes hope into heavy history Convinced to return to the story of Sweet Country, Kaytetye filmmaker Warwick Thornton fell in love with the possibilities.

"Twenty years ago, I look at where the Indigenous film industry was at and it was really out of nowhere," Perkins said.

"Now, we've got Goolagong doing fabulously on the ABC. We've got Wolfram releasing this week. We have Kangaroo, which is co-produced by an Indigenous production company.

"All across the industry, we're really seeing that we have cemented our place in the industry as core to Australian identity and storytelling, which is really to be, you know, something to be really proud of."

For Perkins, the future looks like sustaining this growth and solidifying the industry with support for emerging creators.

"We have to look at the success of the past, what we've changed through being organised, working collectively, looking at government policy, pulling those levers to really chart the future," she said.

"That's a different proposal from what you're talking about in terms of IP, but similar in terms of ensuring that Indigenous content creators, like all Australian content creators, have sustainable careers and that those markets are available to us and that they're guaranteed."

Rachel Perkins with Big and Little Films co-founder Tony Ayres. (Supplied: Screen Producers Australia)

One of the First Nations talents looking to the future is Caden Pearson, a filmmaker and director of Resonant Films, who was crowned one of Screen Producers Australia's One To Watch 2025.

In a reflection of the time it can take to build a profile; Pearson has been in the industry for 12 years but landing on One To Watch was like a "spotlight".

"It's an ultra-marathon in that, unless you're really, really lucky, you don't make it overnight," Pearson told ABC News.

"I have noticed that people that have been achieving things and been in it for a long time, a common theme that I've noticed is that we all have a weird, strong self-belief.

"If you're going to get to where you want to be you have to believe. I know I will get there if I just keep going.

"This must be something, otherwise we would all give up."

World.title: Coaches and fans grumble as technology scrutiny rises
World.content:
In line with the increased professionalism in sport is a drive to be correct as much as possible.

For many, close enough isn't good enough. Seeing your team "robbed" is one of the most heartbreaking experiences a fan can live through.

Last weekend, the concept of correct was tested to the extremes on two prominent occasions. On Sunday afternoon, 60 seconds of football was forgotten to the annals of time at Docklands.

That was the time taken between Rowan Marshall's mark on the line and the umpire blowing the whistle in the middle of the ground signalling a score review had been undertaken.

A few hours later, at Canberra's Manuka Oval, another score review stopped the game in its tracks.

GWS' Xavier O'Halloran booted what in the moment seemed like the match-sealing goal before doubt clouded the ground.

Match-sealer? Let us check that. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

Eighty-five seconds passed between the ball sailing through the posts and the ball being bounced, with players shuffling up and down the ground preparing for a variety of options in the interim.

Unlike the earlier game, O'Halloran's goal was upheld.

The reaction to these incidents was swift from AFL HQ.

"They got that decision correct [Marshall's mark], but it obviously took too long," AFL executive general manager of football operations Greg Swann said on Monday.

AFL boss says umpiring 'as good as it's been' AFL football boss Greg Swann says most of the feedback he receives from the clubs surrounding the officiating in the league is positive despite a pair of controversial review calls in Round 7.

"Going forward now the ARC won't do that. The ARC will still do goal reviews, but they won't intervene in a score like they did on the weekend unless the goal umpire asks for a score review."

The change is the latest in the long line of adjustments the league has made to its score review system since its introduction 15 years ago.

When introduced at the time, then-AFL general manager of football operations Adrian Anderson was clear about the operation of the video assistance.

"Video technology will not remove all errors from the game, as some replays cannot assist, but the aim is to improve decision-making where possible," Anderson said.

At the start, Anderson said that there would be only one to two reviews per game, each causing delays of no more than a minute.

Since then, the system has evolved dramatically.

Instead of obvious errors being the focus, marginal decisions both at and away from the goal line were increasingly being considered.

On at least five separate occasions, changes to the scope or process of score reviews were made during a season, often in the shadow of finals.

These changes often have addressed recent events, such as Adelaide's finals miss in 2023, but not what drives the use of the system and its overall merits.

Criticism of the use of video review in sport, not just the AFL, usually focuses on two elements: the suitability of the technology or the overall need for the assistance and scope for its use.

North Melbourne coach Alastair Clarkson and Giants counterpart Adam Kingsley addressed these issues after GWS' narrow seven-point win.

"I'm not sure it's up to speed yet," Kingsley said.

"It doesn't feel like we're ahead of other sports."

Clarkson said: "I'd prefer there was none [technology] and we just leave it up to the umpires to adjudicate."

Skepticism is growing in sport around video review, and the question of its proper role and scope remains unresolved.

To err is human?

Umpires and players are always going to disagree over calls on-field. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Sport can be complex, with lengthy and detailed rule books. For the most part, things are kept moving by expert adjudicators such as referees or umpires, making decisions on the fly.

But a small subset of decisions are difficult, impactful, controversial and even incorrect.

It's these judgements that are often the trigger for sporting bodies to deploy technology to assist those making rulings on the field. The so-called "howlers" should obviously be corrected, right?

This is an often-repeated justification for the introduction of technological aids such as the AFL's score review system and cricket's Decision Review System (DRS).

In 2019, then-AFL football operations boss Stephen Hocking told SEN: "The score review system was introduced to correct obvious scoring errors."

But how many errors do umpires really make?

Research undertaken by Deakin University showed AFL umpires got about 78 per cent of calls right based on data from the 2016 season.

That may seem high to many fans, but most decisions on the field are not controversial or noteworthy. When umpires got it wrong, they were about twice as likely to miss a call as to pay a free kick erroneously.

This is a stable long-term pattern with earlier data from the AFL in 2000 showing effectively the same accuracy rate.

This 78 per cent accuracy rate for paying free kicks awarded also stacks up reasonably well in a global context, given that research also tends to show physical distance and physical fatigue impact decision-making, factors particularly relevant to Australian football.

The use of technology in sport is designed to reduce this rate where possible. Often the identification of howlers is devolved to players or coaches. Their success rate in doing so is less than ideal.

When given the chance to directly challenge decisions, players and coaches are not significantly better at judging calls.

Such review systems are often about playing the percentages rather than rectifying clear errors. Increasingly, video review is used to not just review the obvious howlers but also tight decisions made at the margins.

West Coast coach Andrew McQualter had an immediate view after his own experiences on Sunday.

"I just think that if they're going to do it, it's got to be clear-cut," he said.

"They've got to get it right. If it's touch and go I would think you're not changing the flow of a game to make a decision like that."

There is also data suggesting that sometimes when a video official intervenes, they make the wrong decision or should not have intervened at all.

According to reporting by the BBC, there were 13 errors made by the video assistant referee (VAR) in the first half of this English Premier League season.

Referees in the Premier League are being put under even more pressure by poor VAR decisions. (Getty Images: Alex Livesey)

These errors, and the delays taken for reviews, have had an impact on fan confidence in the system, with a March survey of 202 having shown that 81 per cent of EPL fans prefer to watch games without VAR.

Academic research also shows that sports officials are quite skilled at getting the easy, more objective calls correct. Unfortunately, it is far more likely that close calls are reviewed than the obvious decisions.

This level of accuracy in both original decision-making and the success of reviews has led to some people questioning the value of these systems.

Clarkson's comments after Sunday's match led to this type of logic.

"There's mistakes by players, there's mistakes by umpires," he said.

"The ball goes through whether it's touched by a fingernail or not, who cares really? Whether it snicks the post or not, who cares really? Just make the call.

"[It's] swings and roundabouts. You are going to win some and you're going to lose some. There seems to be just as much conjecture now as what there always was."

Coaches are starting to wish umpires would stick with their original calls. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Daniel Carson)

Other coaches, such as Luke Beveridge and Damien Hardwick, have echoed this sentiment.

Some fans, players and coaches wish for no use of additional technology, while others advocate for a reduced scope of adoption.

In 2018, then-AFL chief executive Gillon McLachlan was somewhat sympathetic to those feelings in the wake of yet another score review controversy.

"It's not, 'Scrap the whole thing'," McLachlan said at the time.

"It's do we actually finesse it a bit or tone it down and stop trying to solve stuff, which is too hard to do, like a touch from 50 metres, so we'll limit its purview?

"If you did that, then that's a fair conversation. Getting rid of it is not."

There is also the question of whether the technology involved in assisting the umpires is right for the job right now.

Sport, lies and videotape

Fans are increasingly frustrated by the use of technology. (Getty Images: Carl Recine)

Watching the footy, from either the stands or the couch, is a pleasure most of us undertake on a weekly basis.

But sometimes we do not see the whole picture.

Many ordinary sport viewers perhaps do not quite understand the extent to which seemingly infallible video footage can create optical illusions. At a fundamental level, video is a two-dimensional rendering of three-dimensional reality, and certainty is elusive.

Lens zoom and camera angles are big culprits. Cricket viewers are familiar with the dilemma of judging low catches from broadcast footage due to the "foreshortening" effect of a strong zoom making grass, hand and ball nearly impossible to place in three-dimensional space.

Australian football has its own version of this with contentious out-of-bounds judgements around the curved pockets.

Viewers may try forlornly to judge if a ball, while in the air, crossed an imaginary plane over a curved boundary line a few centimetres wide. Often the answer here is simply impossible to discern. As a result, highlights such as Barry Breen's famous point in the 1966 grand final may have been nullified with incorrect use of technology.

Video frame rates and shutter speed also present significant issues for the task of conveying an approximation of reality to an audience.

Consider a football flying quickly towards goal being adjudicated on whether it crossed the back of the goal line before being touched by a defender.

Standard frame rates and shutter speeds can often render balls, arms and digits into a blur, missing the critical moment completely.

Even the high-speed cameras used by the ARC in limited situations last year can struggle to capture the precise moment of a ball crossing the 5-centimetre goal line. Fans and officials often look for signals such as fingers bending back to signal the ball being touched, often without definitive clarity.

Australian football is unique in the way it is played on a large field, with a fast-moving ball and no offside rule or line of scrimmage. These elements make it harder to track the ball than in most sports.

Kingsley touched on issues surrounding technology when speaking after Sunday's match.

Although supportive of the use of technology, Kingsley questioned the current implementation.

"Whether it's the goal line cameras, [or] whether the ball isn't fully across the line … I don't know," Kingsley said.

"[We need to] keep trying to develop as best as you can. You're not going to start with the finished product, so just progressively try and get better and better."

It took a while for Rowan Marshall's mark against the Eagles to be cleared. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Swann indicated in the preseason the league was looking at introducing even more high-frame rate cameras in the coming years.

"We're looking now to upgrade the cameras," Swann told SEN in February.

"There are new cameras out there that we are looking to either purchase or lease that [are] six times better."

There is also more advanced tracking used in some sports, most famously the Hawk-Eye system used in sports such as tennis and cricket.

The hawkeye system, used in cricket and tennis, measures to the millimetre. (Getty Images: Alex Livesey)

These systems use synchronised, fixed cameras to minimise video shortcomings and statistically estimate a trajectory.

Their mere millimetres of error are often cited in their favour, but those error margins mean these systems are responsible for creating an entirely false sense of accuracy and precision.

The Hawk-Eye system works by statistically estimating a ball's position or trajectory based on multiple cameras, but the standard visualisation shows a single location.

A tennis ball might be shown two millimetres out and viewers have no hint that this represents a statistical tie, a null result on a significance test.

The system genuinely cannot say if this ball was out or not.

And that is under ideal conditions. Both cricket and tennis have seen documented situations where larger errors occur due to weather conditions like heat, wind and unusual ball spin.

Cricket's DRS system accounts for this to some degree in its interpretation of LBW decisions, creating an "umpire's call" zone where decisions cannot be confidently predicted.

But few other sports have followed this lead, either in the deployment of Hawk-Eye or other video review systems.

Soccer's notorious VAR renders margins of error into visual certainty even more blatantly. Current applications of off-side technology (SOAT) may have error margins of several centimetres, depending on player speed and the original starting frame for computation.

The EPL has even introduced a five-centimetre buffer to account for these potential errors. It is an error range FIFA has not yet adopted.

Other technologies have also been tested for broader use. The AFL has trialled the use of microchipped balls, while other sports have implemented trials using local and global positioning systems.

Many of these efforts have shown limited success to date. But the use of embedded microphones, such as AFL's Edge and cricket's Snicko, have been far more accepted and successful.

This technological advancement, however, may not be enough to silence all of the doubters.

Moving forward

It is rare for technological advancements to be completely removed once introduced, but it is not uncommon for their use to be constrained or expanded further.

Nevertheless, there is a sizeable cohort of fans and officials calling for further review of video review.

Is all the extra noise around umpire reviews worth it? (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

"The game is chaotic, it's not black and white," Beveridge told reporters this week.

"Ultimately, if there's confusion as to who it went off, what did we used to do? We used to ball it in.

"How about we just ball it in again? People are going to make mistakes. And it might have come off someone's boot.

"But no, we have to bring another layer in, and now we have to reverse it."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Simplification and a tolerance of uncertainty may be hard to enact, but many fans, players and officials have a desire to return to the game from their youth, which did not have score review.

There is a serious argument for the game to be decided on the field by those there at the time and let uncertainty be part of the experience.

Doubting the judgement of on-field umpires also has flow-on effects to the trust in their non-reviewable decisions.

Some studies involving elite football players have even indicated players feel a sense of frustration and anxiety relating to the constant monitoring by VAR.

Some players mentioned they felt referees had been disempowered by the use of technology.

Beyond this nostalgia-driven desire, there are real questions surrounding the scope of video review and the problems — howlers or general calls — that the system is trying to resolve.

The AFL will have to work hard to find a middle ground to placate all of its stakeholders in the years to come.

World.title: Australia news live: Chaos erupts overnight at Alice Springs Hospital as man arrested over death of Kumanjayi Little Baby; Trump floats new plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
Ahead of next week’s Farrer byelection, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has criticised the Liberal and National parties’ preferencing of One Nation over independent candidate Michelle Milthorpe.

“One Nation would not have the opportunity to be successful were it not for the decision of the Liberal Party and the National Party to support One Nation by giving the One Nation candidate preferences,” Albanese said.

“That’s something that is completely contradictory to what John Howard did when he was prime minister, when One Nation were on the rise, way back in 1998 before they collapsed. One Nation has a history of people being elected to Parliament, including here in New South Wales, such as Mark Latham, and then there being a breakdown in those relationships.”

Albanese said the reason a byelection was taking place on May 9, was because men in the Liberal Party had deposed their first female leader, Sussan Ley.

“People got together and removed Sussan Ley as the leader of the Liberal Party before she even had a chance to give a budget reply, and she was never given an opportunity,” Albanese said.

“The men in the Liberal Party gathered on the day of a funeral of one of their former colleagues in order to discuss who would replace Sussan Ley as the leader of the Liberal Party. And they didn’t give her a chance. That’s why this byelection is occurring.”

World.title: I was in the middle of the riot when the tear gas struck. Then an angry man confronted me
World.content:
First person NationalCrime I was in the middle of the riot when the tear gas struck. Then an angry man confronted me Hannah Murphy Updated May 1, 2026 — 12:48pm ,first published May 1, 2026 — 8:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains an image of a deceased Indigenous person. Alice Springs: We got the word Jefferson Lewis had been arrested just as I’d finally put my head down to sleep. It had been a huge day. We started it with Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family, sitting with them in their home in Old Timers Camp. They were still immensely sad, but were hopeful on what would have been the fifth day of the Northern Territory police and state emergency services search for the missing five-year-old. Community members protest outside the Alice Springs Hospital. Sam Mooy The young girl had disappeared on Anzac Day, and was last seen in the company of Jefferson Lewis – a 47-year-old man who had recently got out of prison.



Police immediately zeroed in on Lewis as a potential kidnapper, but it was only on Thursday afternoon that we got the news everyone had dreaded: her body had been found. Loading We went to the crime scene, and among the buffel grass contemplated how a tiny girl would have felt out here in the company of a near stranger. When we got back to our hotel, ready to finally turn in for the evening, shouts started up on the Alice Springs streets below. “They got him! He’s at the hospital!”



A woman ran over from another balcony to show me a livestream of people gathering outside the Alice Springs Hospital, surrounding the front car park of the building. Photographer Sam Mooy and I ran to our car and headed down there ourselves – and what we saw was described by one bystander as the “biggest thing” they’d ever seen in Alice Springs. Hundreds of people crowded the street, throwing things at police, screaming hatred for the man who had been locked away inside. Lewis had been taken straight to the hospital because he had been found by police beaten at a nearby Charles Creek residence.



Some in the crowd wanted blood, and demanded it. A police van is set on fire. Sam Mooy Photo: Sam Mooy Tear gas was fired into the angry crowd of protesters. Sam Mooy Photo: Sam Mooy



Police responded by first holding the line and blocking all access to the hospital, but the shouts got louder, and bricks began to be hurled. Officers ducked behind their cars, which had their window shields smashed and repeatedly kicked by what looked like young children. Men screamed for Lewis to be brought out – “so we can all go home”. Those in the crowd said they wanted to deal with him their way. They were furious with police for “protecting him”, and a kind Aboriginal liaison officer in his 70s who had been looking after the family and had consoled me earlier outside their residence took the brunt of their anger. Kumanjayi Little Baby. Soon, police began to respond. A woman used me as a human shield to avoid a rubber bullet being shot at us, and bodies collapsed around us as tear gas spread.



I piggybacked a seven-year-old boy across the road and back to his mother as tears streamed down his face, crying out the pepper spray. I was soon to follow, coughing and spluttering with my hands on my knees as a kind man offered me some water in his car. Related Article Crime Jefferson Lewis was beaten before his arrest. This is how the riot began About midnight and after two hours of rioting, we called it and jumped into the car for safety, but then an irate man pounded on our hood and told us to leave. We didn’t understand his urgency until we saw a police car behind us go up in flames. It was hard to tell if the series of booms that followed was from the rubber bullets being fired, glass shattering or the interior of the police car burning. I could only watch on as another cameraman took a face full of spray, and had his eyes washed out by a journalist from another outlet. A bin was set on fire. Rocks were thrown at police. Men pulled shirts over their faces and children had water poured over their eyes.



But still, Lewis remained inside. For all the screaming, throwing, crying – police have every intention of bringing the man they say murdered Kumanjayi Little Baby to justice. Our Breaking News Alert will notify you of significant breaking news when it happens. Get it here.

World.title: Police called to polling booth as Sydney council vote descends into chaos
World.content:
Exclusive NationalNSWSydney councils Police called to polling booth as Sydney council vote descends into chaos Anthony Segaert Updated May 1, 2026 — 12:30pm ,first published April 16, 2026 — 5:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A toxic south-west Sydney council byelection has descended into chaos after police were called to a polling booth amid a screaming match between a councillor and a candidate. The altercation came a day after Liverpool City Council’s Liberal mayor accidentally published the former home address of the area’s Labor state MP in a Facebook video criticising circumstances which led to the south ward byelection, triggered by the resignation of deputy mayor Betty Green in January. Liverpool Liberal councillor Richard Ammoun and independent byelection candidate Jamal Daoud were seen shouting at each other at pre-poll at Casula Community Centre on Thursday afternoon. Police at the Casula Community Centre pre-poll station. Daoud, who ran as an independent for the seat of Werriwa in last year’s federal election, claimed he was called a liar by Ammoun for alleging there was corruption at the council, and that a Liberal supporter said in Arabic “your father is a son of a bitch”.



An electoral worker inside then called NSW Police, Daoud and other witnesses confirmed. “I needed at that time to say a few bad words about him,” Daoud told the Herald on Thursday afternoon. “Not bad, but I said ‘Shut your mouth’, or something like that. You can’t talk about my father like this, especially [because] he is a dead person now.” Jamal Daoud, an independent candidate, now wears a bodycam at the pre-poll station. Anthony Segaert Ammoun said Daoud was lying about there being corruption at the council. “He was just saying things that were untrue to constituents, I tried to correct him,” Ammoun said. “He started calling me names in his native language. I remained calm, even while the police were there.”



Daoud is now wearing a bodycam for the final few days of the campaign. A NSW Police spokesperson said they were called regarding a civil matter and left without incident. State MP’s former address posted online The incident is the latest escalation in a dramatic 24 hours ahead of Saturday’s vote, which will return about 82,000 of the council’s residents to the polls. On Wednesday night, Liberal mayor Ned Mannoun posted an extraordinary 3-minute and 50-second video to Facebook of him sitting in front of a corkboard containing the faces of his political rivals connected by pins and a piece of string, discussing “the cold, hard truth” about the council.



Ned Mannoun, mayor of Liverpool, posted the video about his political rivals late on Wednesday night. Facebook/Ned Mannoun - Mayor of Liverpool For about three seconds, as Mannoun was talking about the United Services Union’s donations to Labor, a photo appeared on-screen of an election donation disclosure form which revealed unredacted addresses of Liverpool’s state Labor MP Charishma Kaliyanda and Green. Kaliyanda, a former Liverpool councillor, said it was “doxxing”. “I’m getting advice about what my options are,” she said. “Does this mean that I need to move house? What does this mean in terms of safety and security measures that I need to put in place for myself and my family?” Kaliyanda later confirmed she had not lived at the address for several years, but in a separate statement said she had concerns for her safety.



Mannoun stopped short of apologising for sharing the data in the video but said: “I’m sorry that a publicly available document was published.” The people whose addresses were shared weren’t mentioned in the video, and the size of the clipping was barely legible, Mannoun said. On Thursday morning, he removed the video and re-uploaded it with the information blurred. Mannoun said he was planning to publish more social media content about the saga. “Wait for my next video,” he said. CLARIFICATION This story has been updated after Labor MP Charishma Kaliyanda confirmed she no longer lives at the address that Liverpool Mayor Ned Mannoun made public.

World.title: What style of wine − and how many bottles − should you take to a dinner party?
World.content:
Assuming it’s OK to take wine to a dinner party (some hosts may be offended), my recommendation is to take one bottle, not three. If your friends are thirsty types, though, three might, indeed, be the way to go.

What to choose? Ideally, suit the wine to the meal, your host and the other guests. Take a hearty shiraz if it’s a wintertime barbecue or a semillon if it’s a summertime seafood alfresco deal.

If your host has a show-off cellar, you can’t possibly compete, so take something eccentric, such as a Hungarian harslevelu or Georgian mtsvane. A bottle of Grange will always be a hit if your pockets are that deep.

World.title: Rail network loses 273 services, commuters warned of slower, crowded trains
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Rail Rail network loses 273 services, commuters warned of slower, crowded trains Courtney Kruk May 1, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

South-east Queensland commuters have been warned to expect delayed services, longer travel times and crowded trains from next week as a wage dispute between unions and the state government continues. From Tuesday, the rail network will run with 273 fewer services – a capacity of about 80 per cent – on a timetable similar to those offered on Saturdays. South-east Queensland train commuters have been warned of further disruptions to services from Tuesday. Courtney Kruk This will mean 15-minute services for the Gold Coast, Cleveland, Redcliffe Peninsula, Springfield, Ferny Grove, Caboolture and Ipswich lines, a drop from usual services every six to 10 minutes. Other lines including Shorncliffe, Beenleigh, the Sunshine Coast between Caboolture and Nambour, Rosewood and Eagle Junction will run every 30 minutes.



Related Article Queensland Rail ‘Stonewalled on every claim’: Rail staff reject pay offer, vow more action Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said efforts were being made to reduce the impact on lines with the greatest patronage, including extra services during peak morning and afternoon periods, but he warned commuters to expect disruptions. “The trains will be more crowded [and] it will be slower as more people are required to move in and out of the trains,” he said. Outside of peak hours, trains are expected to operate on 30-minute intervals instead of 15 minutes. Services were being reduced as a result of “a backlog of maintenance, unaddressed service faults and delays to critical component overhaul projects”, which Mickelberg said was a direct consequence of industrial action by the unions.



“Queensland Rail is, and continues to be, ready to deliver services that Queenslanders expect, and the reason they haven’t been able to do that is because of union activity,” he said. “So my message to the unions today is, stop your strike action. Get back to work and get back to the negotiating table.” Queensland Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said reduced services were a direct result of union action and maintenance backlog, with not enough “rolling stock” for the network. Courtney Kruk Queensland Rail chief executive Kat Stapleton said she shared the frustration of commuters who had faced disruptions in recent weeks. “Queensland Rail wants to run a full timetable, but we can’t do that during this continued union-protected industrial action,” Stapleton said.



Seven unions connected to rail services are engaged in wage negotiations with Queensland Rail. All rejected the government’s latest offer at a Fair Work Commission meeting on Monday, and vowed to continue “low-level action” causing “minor disruptions” in coming weeks. Related Article Queensland government Minister refuses to apologise for rail delays ahead of limited reprieve Mickelberg said union action to date affected Queensland Rail’s “rolling stock”, with many trains still offline. Because of this, a decision had been made to issue parts of the rail maintenance workforce with section 471 notices, meaning they will not be paid if works are not completed.



“Those who are striking right now, if you’re not doing your job, we won’t be paying,” Mickelberg said. “If this is not a lockout, we welcome the rail maintenance workforce coming back to work and doing their job, in which case they will be paid.” Union representatives are due to meet with Queensland Rail again on May 7. Comment has been sought from unions. Queensland Rail said the network’s Journey Planner would be updated overnight. Mickelberg said extra bus services would be deployed to fill gaps, but noted constraints given the time of year.



Reduced services timetable: From Tuesday, May 5, trains will run similar to a Saturday timetable, with extra services in the morning and afternoon peak, until further notice. Gold Coast line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Cleveland line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Redcliffe Peninsula line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Springfield line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak Ipswich line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Ferny Grove: Running to Roma Street every 15 minutes in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Caboolture line: 15-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 30-minute services off peak

Shorncliffe line: 30-minute services all day

Beenleigh line: 30-minute services all day

Sunshine Coast line (between Caboolture and Nambour): 30-minute services in the morning and afternoon peaks, 90-minutes off peak (as per normal timetable)

Rosewood – Ipswich shuttle: 30-minute service all day

Doomben – Eagle Junction shuttle: 30-minute service all day

Airtrain services are unaffected Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Watch: Dyson Daniels ejected for elbow after fiery NBA brawl
World.content:
SportBasketballNBA Watch: Dyson Daniels ejected for elbow after fiery NBA brawl Jon Pierik May 1, 2026 — 12:05pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australian basketball star Dyson Daniels and his Atlanta Hawks have shown some fight, but it ended in ejections on a night the New York Knicks produced a record-breaking performance to advance into the second round of the NBA play-offs on Friday (AEST). Frustrations boiled over with 4:39 minutes left in the second quarter of game six of their first-round playoff series at State Farm Arena when Daniels and Knicks centre Mitchell Robinson became entangled during a set of free throws. Loading With the Hawks trailing by an all-time play-offs record 47 points, Robinson took umbrage when Daniels appeared to elbow him, prompting Robinson to get into the face of the dogged guard. Players and officials rushed over to separate the pair. The fight spilled over into the front row of fans, appearing to involve most of the on-court members of both teams.



Related Article NBL ‘Deeply troubling’: Basketball’s battle of the billionaires reignites After the referees reviewed footage, Daniels and Robinson were given technical fouls and ejected from the game. During the skirmish, one of the referees fell to the floor. Veteran commentator Mike Breen, calling the action on ESPN, quickly noted Robinson’s frustration. “Oh, and Robinson and Dyson just being held up … Brett Barneke gets knocked down! Robinson wants to go after somebody,” he said. “They’re trying to separate the two. Robinson really upset. The frustrations coming through for the Hawks right now.”



It was a dirty night for the Hawks, who trailed 3-2 in the series and had been trying to keep their season alive. The Knicks led 83–36 at halftime, the largest half-time deficit ever in an NBA playoff game, and went on to win 140-89. This was the largest score by the Knicks in play-off history. Tough guys: Australian star Dyson Daniels and New York Knicks centre Mitchell Robinson get up close and personal in game six of their play-off series. Both men were ejected. AP Centre Karl Anthony-Towns had a triple double of 12 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists, OG Anunoby had a team-high 29 points, while playmaker Jalen Brunson had 17 points and eight assists. Daniels had three points in 15 minutes before his ejection. Guard Jalen Johnson led the Hawks with 21 points, while star shooter CJ McCollum, the hero of games two and three, was held to only 11 points on 4-13 shooting from the floor.



The Knicks play the winner of the series between Boston and Philadelphia. Game six is later on Friday (AEST). News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: Man charged with attempted murder after paramedic stabbed in face and neck
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCrime Man charged with attempted murder after paramedic stabbed in face and neck Lachlan Abbott and Erin Pearson Updated May 1, 2026 — 12:02pm ,first published May 1, 2026 — 7:23am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The man accused of stabbing an on-duty paramedic in the face and neck outside a Melbourne cafe has faced court after being charged with attempted murder. Mohamud Ali, 32, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Friday for a brief hearing where no application for bail was made. Loading The court heard it was Ali’s first time in custody, and was told he needed access to diazepam which his treating doctor had earlier prescribed. The court heard that no diagnoses were to be put on the court file.



Magistrate Donna Bakos ordered Ali return to court on August 6. Earlier, police alleged the 32-year-old stopped his car outside the Reservoir cafe on Broadway just after 11am on Thursday, jumped out and stabbed the paramedic in the upper body. The on-duty paramedic, who had stopped for a coffee, performed first aid on himself before help arrived. He was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries. “Investigators allege a male got out of a small, red car and stabbed the paramedic to the upper body before fleeing in the vehicle,” police said in a statement.



The alleged offender was arrested in Winter Crescent, Reservoir, just before 1pm on Thursday and charged later that night. The attack prompted the Allan government to reveal it planned to strengthen the law to make jail mandatory in all circumstances for people who assault emergency services workers. Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery addressed the media with union secretary Danny Hill (right) and other paramedics on Thursday. Alexander Darling Injuring an emergency worker has been a category 1 offence requiring a prison sentence since 2018, but this masthead revealed in February a man had avoided jail despite hospitalising a female paramedic as she was not treating a patient when she was attacked. The ambulance union has since been lobbying the Victorian government to close the loophole.



The paramedic, a 20-year-old man originally from the Northern Territory, remained in Royal Melbourne Hospital’s emergency department on Thursday night in a serious but stable condition. Related Article Crime Victoria to overhaul penalty laws after on-duty paramedic stabbed in face, neck Ambulance Victoria chief executive Jordan Emery said the attack was random, unprovoked, and took place while the victim was getting out of his vehicle. “It is completely unacceptable that people who spend their lives caring for others – who give so much to care for their communities – continue to face violence on a daily basis,” he said on Thursday afternoon, flanked by a dozen paramedics outside the Royal Melbourne Hospital. Emery said a bystander had intervened to stop the offender, which allowed the paramedic to perform first aid on himself – despite bleeding profusely – until his colleagues arrived.
